Volume 11 · Chapter 02

Bank balance sheets, capital and liquidity

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v11-c01

By the endReconcile bank accounts and distinguish liquidity shortages from insolvency.

Reconcile the accounts before judging the bank

Capability. Reconstruct a bank's balance sheet from transactions, reconcile income with equity, and distinguish an allowance, loss-absorbing funding, economic net worth and cash available at a payment deadline. Then compare capital measures and test a dated funding plan without counting the same asset twice. The prerequisite is financial intermediation and bank economics, together with the accounting identities from Volume 7 and dated valuation from Volume 10.

Alder Bank reports positive equity, receives a loan recovery and owns securities worth more than its next wholesale repayment. It nevertheless cannot execute its proposed payment plan. The diagnosis requires the amount and timing of accessible cash, the claims already secured on those securities, and the meaning of the reported equity. Adding all favorable numbers to one “buffer” would obscure the problem.

All cases are original synthetic examples in currency units (CU), for one legal entity and one currency. Our simplified ledger uses cost amounts for securities, gross contractual loan balances less a positive allowance, no taxes, no other comprehensive income and no unrecorded transaction unless stated. It is a teaching convention, not a complete accounting standard or a regulatory return. Actual national capital definitions and regulation are developed in Chapter 10; the ratios and thresholds below are expressly instructional.

1. Four quantities that answer different questions

Write C for cash and settlement balances, B for securities at their book amount, G for gross loans, A for the credit-loss allowance, O for other book assets, D for deposits, W for wholesale borrowing, P for other liabilities and E for book equity. Here A is a contra-asset: an account subtracted from gross loans, not a cash account. In this chapter the letter A always means the allowance; write TA for total assets.

Net loans = G−A;   TA=C+B+G−A+O;
TA = D+W+P+E;   E = TA−(D+W+P).

A deposit is an asset of its customer and a liability of the bank. Equity is the residual funding claim after liabilities; cash is an asset that can settle a payment when it is usable. Neither the label “reserves” nor the word “buffer” identifies which account is meant. Central-bank settlement balances, an allowance for losses, and accumulated retained earnings have different entries and different uses.

State the measurement before interpreting the number
QuantityQuestion it addressesWhat it does not establish
Book equityWhat residual follows from the specified accounting amounts?Current sale proceeds or payment capacity
Economic equityWhat residual follows from a stated common-date asset/liability valuation?A legally executable cash receipt or an observed probability of failure
A capital ratioHow large is a defined numerator relative to a defined exposure denominator?Which payment can be made before its cutoff
Dated liquidity headroomCan available receipts and funding cover due cash under stated rights?Positive economic net worth or resilience to every unmodeled scenario

The Bank of England's September 2013 UK primer is useful conceptual background for the distinction between capital funding and liquid assets. Its historical regulatory figures and incurred-loss accounting discussion are not current requirements adopted here. We derive our results from the explicit accounts and contracts below.

2. Follow both sides of every transaction

A loan credited to the borrower's deposit raises G and D by the same amount. Cash need not change at origination. When the borrower pays someone at another bank, the originating bank transfers settlement cash and reduces its deposit liability. Payment to another customer at the same bank instead reallocates deposit ownership without changing aggregate D or C. These entries do not imply unlimited lending: cash settlement, credit risk, capital, profitability and other constraints still matter.

Collecting existing loan principal from outside the bank exchanges a loan asset for cash. Cash interest received is revenue in this stipulated case; it raises cash and current earnings. Interest credited to a customer's deposit is an expense and an increase in the deposit liability; it does not immediately transfer settlement cash. A dividend reduces cash and equity but is not an operating expense. We assume the dividend is contractually permitted in the example; its prudence is a separate decision.

Eend = Estart + net income − dividends + paid-in equity,
when there are no other direct equity movements.

The identity is a reconciliation, not a statement that earnings always arrive as cash. Accrued interest, for example, could raise an interest receivable and income without an immediate receipt; this lab deliberately uses collected interest to keep its ledger bounded. Always inspect the entry supporting the reported profit.

3. Provision, charge-off and recovery are separate events

A provision p in our ledger increases A by p and reduces earnings and E by p. No settlement cash moves. A charge-off c covered by an existing allowance reduces both G and A by c. Consequently (G−c)−(A−c)=G−A: net loans, total assets and equity do not fall a second time. The borrower has not repaid c; the accounting records the removal of an amount already provided for.

This neutrality requires sufficient allowance. If an unprovided loss is discovered, recognize the additional loss; one cannot preserve equity by writing a negative contra-asset balance and calling it a covered charge-off. Nor does accounting neutrality mean that new default information is economically harmless. A valuation or forecast may change when the information arrives, even if a later bookkeeping step merely uses an existing allowance.

For this positive-allowance case, a cash recovery r of an already charged-off amount is recorded as a cash debit and an allowance credit. Thus C and A both rise by r; current recovery income and E do not change. The allowance is then reassessed. If the supported ending target is lower, an explicitly recorded allowance release raises earnings. The receipt and the reassessment must not both be silently treated as the same income gain.

Aend = Astart + provision − charge-offs + recoveries − releases.
With no separate release: provision = Aend−Astart+charge-offs−recoveries.

A dated primary reference is the United States interagency policy statement of 1 June 2020, whose allowance overview distinguishes valuation accounts, periodic provision adjustments and write-offs. Its scope includes qualifications absent from our model, including circumstances involving expected recoveries and negative allowances. Our nonnegative-allowance restriction is a lab boundary, not a universal assertion about that policy or current GAAP.

Worked example 1 — The same bank through ten entries

Alder opens with cash 40, securities 60, gross loans 240, allowance 8, property 6 and goodwill 2. Assets are 40+60+240−8+6+2=340. Deposits are 260, wholesale borrowing 50 and other liabilities 10, leaving equity 20. The securities comprise book amounts 40 currently free and 20 already pledged. Neither property nor goodwill is cash.

Post the following entries in order. Collections and payments described as cash cross the bank boundary. The recovery concerns a previously charged-off amount, and the supported allowance after all ten entries is 5. Securities, property, goodwill, wholesale borrowing and other liabilities do not change in this journal.

Account balances after each stipulated entry; all amounts in CU
EntryCash CGross GAllowance ADeposits DEquity E
Opening40240826020
1. Lend 20 by crediting deposit40260828020
2. Borrower transfers 16 externally24260826420
3. Collect principal 8 externally32252826420
4. Collect cash interest 537252826425
5. Credit deposit interest 237252826623
6. Pay salaries 1.5 in cash35.5252826621.5
7. Record provision 635.52521426615.5
8. Charge off 10 against allowance35.5242426615.5
9. Recover 1; credit allowance36.5242526615.5
10. Pay dividend 234.5242526613.5

Ending net loans are 242−5=237. Assets are 34.5+60+237+8=339.5, while liabilities 266+50+10=326 plus equity 13.5 give the same total. Every intermediate row also balances when the unchanged accounts are included.

Income is 5−2−1.5−6=−4.5. Equity reconciles as 20−4.5−2=13.5. The allowance reconciles as 8+6−10+1=5. Cash instead changes by −16+8+5−1.5+1−2=−5.5, ending at 34.5. The three reconciliations have different terms because they measure different things. Charging the 10 write-off to earnings again would count the recognized loss twice; adding allowance 5 to cash would invent an asset.

4. Book equity and economic net worth use different valuations

Let VA and VL be asset and liability values at one common date, using a declared valuation basis and the actual cash rights. Economic equity is Eecon=VA−VL. If a loan portfolio is supplied as a complete present value, do not subtract its accounting allowance again unless the supplied valuation explicitly excludes those losses. The book allowance and an economic loss estimate are not two automatically additive deductions.

Values depend on discounting, credit, optionality, market liquidity and the intended valuation question. A stressed liquidation price, a going-concern present value and a recent accounting carrying amount need not coincide. Here economic values are stipulated common-date scenario marks; liabilities are valued at their carrying amounts and no own-credit gain, franchise value or new business is introduced. A negative residual means balance-sheet insolvency under this specified valuation, not a legal determination. A positive residual does not ensure today’s bills can be paid.

Eecon−Ebook = Σ(asset economic value−book value)
−Σ(liability economic value−book value).

A loss on an asset reduces the residual available to equity if liabilities retain their value. If economic values are uncertain, report the assumptions and range. An adverse mark is not itself an observed probability or a forecast of tomorrow's forced-sale proceeds.

5. A numerator and a denominator, not a pile of cash

The simple book-equity ratio E/TA measures book equity per unit of book assets. Its inverse TA/E is meaningful as a positive leverage multiple only when E>0. A risk-weighted measure instead uses R=ΣwiXi, where exposures X and weights w must be defined. Weighted exposures need not be market losses, expected losses or cash outflows. Changing a weight can change a reported ratio without changing a single contract.

For our invented policy, define adjusted capital K=E−goodwill; adjusted exposure U=TA−goodwill; and R=1·net loans+0.20·book securities+1·property. Cash has zero weight and goodwill is deducted from K and U rather than also weighted in R. Require K/R≥6% and K/U≥4%. These are toy gates, not CET1, an actual regulatory leverage ratio, or an applicable national minimum. A real calculation would require eligible-instrument rules, deductions, consolidation, exposure definitions, off-balance-sheet treatment and the jurisdiction's effective date.

A cash equity issue of x changes K to K+x, U to U+x and, under these weights, leaves R unchanged. The minimum amount meeting both toy ratios is therefore

xcapital = max{0, 0.06R−K, (0.04U−K)/(1−0.04)}.

This follows by multiplying each inequality by its positive denominator; the cash proceeds must enter U. If stable deposits are instead converted into equity, assets and U do not change, deposits fall by x and K rises by x. Its leverage requirement is x≥0.04U−K. Such a conversion adds no cash. New borrowing from outside adds cash and a liability, leaving E and K unchanged; in this example it increases U and therefore reduces K/U.

Worked example 2 — Three views of the closing balance sheet

At the closing date, the free securities have economic value 36, the already pledged pool 20, net loans a complete economic value 231, property 6 and goodwill 0. Cash remains 34.5; liabilities remain 326. Thus economic assets are 327.5 and economic equity 1.5. Relative to book equity 13.5, the deductions are securities 4, loans 6 and goodwill 2: total 12. In a separate adverse loan valuation of 223, economic equity is −6.5. Neither mark changes the cash ledger just by being calculated.

The book-equity ratio is 13.5/339.5≈3.9764%. The invented capital measures are K=11.5, U=337.5 and R=237+12+6=255. Hence K/R≈4.5098% and K/U≈3.4074%, below both toy gates. Cash equity must cover at least 15.3−11.5=3.8 for the first gate and (13.5−11.5)/.96=25/12≈2.083333 for the second. The binding amount is 3.8.

After that cash issue, K=15.3 and U=341.3, giving 6% and approximately 4.4829%. Book equity is 17.3; base economic equity rises to 5.3. Under the adverse loan mark it is still −2.7. Passing these invented ratio thresholds does not certify every valuation scenario or the legal sufficiency of capital.

6. Liquidity belongs to an entity, an asset and a deadline

Cash that is restricted cannot automatically be spent. Securities already pledged cannot be pledged again unless the relevant agreements actually permit reuse and a lender accepts it. Even free securities require an executable sale or borrowing arrangement, the right settlement date, and an eligible counterparty. A haircut h on collateral value M permits a stipulated cash advance (1−h)M. That financing deduction is not automatically an accounting expense or a fall in the asset's economic value.

Do not add both sale proceeds and collateralized borrowing proceeds from the same full asset position. A collateralized loan leaves the asset and a new borrowing liability on the balance sheet; a sale removes the asset and recognizes any difference between proceeds and book carrying amount under our stipulated rules. A later collateral release requires satisfaction of the secured obligation. The BCBS's September 2008 international liquidity principles provide method context for dated cash projections, transfer restrictions and collateral availability; they do not promise a facility to this fictional bank or establish a national-law test.

For a fixed feasible borrowing/sale plan, define Hj as unrestricted cash after all receipts and payments at cutoff j. Each receipt must arrive before the payment that relies on it. An internal desired cash floor is a further policy requirement, not automatically an unpaid obligation. We distinguish them explicitly: a negative H means the proposed payments cannot all be made without accessing restricted cash or new funding; H below a positive management target but above zero means a target breach.

Hj = initial unrestricted cash + cumulative timely receipts
+ cumulative new funding − cumulative due payments − cumulative funding repayments.

Prefix feasibility. In this deterministic fixed-plan setting, with all receipts settled before each listed cutoff and no unlisted constraint, Hj≥0 at every cutoff is necessary and sufficient to complete the plan. Necessity follows from cash conservation; sufficiency follows by carrying each nonnegative remainder to the next cutoff. A later positive remainder does not repair an earlier failure. If an external cash injection x arrives before all cutoffs and changes no other modeled cash, the minimum required injection is maxj{0,−Hj}. This is a narrow cash certificate, not an optimization over uncertain funding choices.

Worked example 3 — Positive value, a missed cutoff, and three different repairs

Continue from Alder's closing book accounts. Of cash 34.5, 4.5 is legally unavailable throughout the horizon, leaving 30 usable. At cutoff 1, loan principal 10 arrives before payments of 50 deposits, 15 wholesale debt and 5 of the already-recorded other liabilities: total 70. The 5 is within the existing other-liability balance 10, not a new expense or an internal desired floor.

A committed new secured facility arrives by cutoff 1 and lends 80% of the free securities' value 36, or 28.8. The entire free pool is then pledged until repayment. The old pledged pool, valued at 20, supports other debt and cannot be reused. No securities sale, unsecured credit or external contribution is available in the base plan. Usable cash is 30+10+28.8=68.8, giving a 1.2 payment shortfall despite base economic equity 1.5.

At cutoff 2 an additional 12 of loan principal arrives and 5 deposits are due. At cutoff 3 another 25 of principal arrives; the new secured loan must be repaid at gross factor 1.01, totaling 29.088, including interest 0.288. All other claims mature outside this horizon. Under the hypothetical assumption that every payment could be made, unrestricted remainders are −1.2, 5.8 and 1.712. The last two are diagnostic projections, not an executable history: the plan already failed at cutoff 1. A recovery or loan receipt arriving at cutoff 2 cannot travel backward in time.

Alternative 3.8-CU repairs completed before cutoff 1; compare from the same closing ledger
RepairBook equityCash addedToy risk / leverage ratioFirst cash headroom
Outside investor pays cash for equity17.33.86% / 4.4829%+2.6
Stable deposits converted to equity17.306% / 4.5333%−1.2
New external unsecured borrowing13.53.84.5098% / 3.3695%+2.6

The converted deposits are explicitly excluded from the scheduled 55 deposit outflows, so conversion does not reduce this plan's payments. The new unsecured borrowing matures after cutoff 3 and has no in-horizon interest payment; its later obligations are not eliminated. The cash issue passes the two toy ratios and the three displayed cash cutoffs, whose remainders become 2.6, 9.6 and 5.512. After all scheduled payments, that variant has cash 10.012, gross loans 195, allowance 5, securities 60, property/goodwill 8, deposits 211, wholesale debt 35, other liabilities 5 and equity 17.012. Assets 268.012 equal liabilities 251 plus equity. Secured interest, not principal repayment, reduced equity by 0.288.

These comparisons isolate mechanisms. Funding access does not itself recapitalize a bank; an accounting recapitalization does not always bring settlement cash. A plan approved against one asset valuation, haircut and timeline must be reconsidered when those inputs or legal rights change.

7. Reproducible ledger and stress lab

The lab guide documents the synthetic inputs, standard-library Python model, saved base output and file manifest. The quiet run(data) API does not mutate its input. From the downloaded project directory, run python3 v11-c02-analysis.py v11-c02-inputs.json; -O preserves validation.

The model records every journal balance, income/equity reconciliation, common-date economic marks, defined capital ratios and the cash plan. It marks the first failed cutoff and keeps subsequent full-payment projections visibly conditional. It does not optimize loan sales, infer credit losses, provide regulatory capital or guarantee access to a real lender. Tests should alter transactions, timing, haircuts and information, not merely compare a saved file with itself.

Before trusting a result, reconcile amounts to contracts, explain each counter-entry, verify collateral ownership and settlement capability, and distinguish a measured loss from a scenario. An independent reviewer should reconstruct the allowance roll-forward, all cash prefixes and the economic-value bridge from source records. An exactly balanced spreadsheet can still omit a liability or value the wrong cash rights.

Exercises

  1. Loan creation and settlement. Starting from the closing Alder ledger, lend 12 by crediting a customer's deposit. The customer transfers 5 to another bank and 7 to another Alder customer. Give every aggregate account change and the new total assets, liabilities, equity, cash and gross loans. Explain why the two payments have different aggregate cash effects.
  2. Allowance reconstruction. A separate portfolio begins with gross loans 70 and allowance 6. During the period charge-offs are 8, cash recoveries of previously written-off loans are 1, and the supported final allowance is 5. No originations, principal receipts or other income occur. Determine the provision, a valid sequence of entries, final net loans and changes in cash, total assets and equity. Why would charging both provision and charge-off to income be wrong?
  3. Valuation basis. Keep Alder's closing cash, security marks, other asset marks and liability values from Worked example 2. Derive economic equity as a function of a complete loan-portfolio value L. Find the zero-equity threshold. Evaluate L=231 and L=223. A colleague additionally deducts allowance 5 from each result; identify the duplicated item and state when a separate adjustment would instead be needed.
  4. A changed weight is not a new asset. Without changing any contract, cash, book amount or economic value, replace only the toy loan weight 1 by 0.70. Compute R and both toy capital ratios. Does either gate change? Explain what this calculation does and does not establish about loss absorption, and identify one reason an actual risk-weight change would require evidence beyond an arithmetic improvement.
  5. Deadline and haircut. For the base cash plan, derive the largest haircut on free value 36 consistent with the cutoff-1 payments. Reconcile all three base headrooms. If the 12 principal receipt originally at cutoff 2 were contractually moved before cutoff 1, leaving all other flows and the 20% haircut fixed, find all three new headrooms. Explain why aggregating the original three cutoffs into one final cash balance gives the wrong feasibility conclusion.
  6. Choose the repair. Derive the minimum external cash equity issue that satisfies both original toy capital gates and every base cash cutoff. Compare a deposit conversion and borrowing of that amount, respecting the stated stable-deposit and maturity assumptions. Calculate the cash issue's post-repair severe economic equity. Give a decision limited to the evidence actually supplied.
  7. Sale instead of pledge. Replace the new secured facility entirely with a sale of the whole free securities pool: book 40, economic mark 36, executable proceeds 34 arriving before cutoff 1. No new secured loan is drawn or later repaid; all other scheduled cash is unchanged. Compute the sale's book loss, new book equity, immediate economic-equity change relative to the supplied mark, and all three cash headrooms. Explain how a liquidity repair can worsen solvency, and why adding the 28.8 facility as well would be invalid.
  8. Audit and teach the error. A report claims first-cutoff headroom is 34.5+5+10+0.8(56)−70=24.3, says a positive book-equity figure independently certifies safety, and cites the 2013 primer as if its accounting recognition discussion were a current universal rule. Identify and quantify every overstatement in that headroom calculation. Write a short correction specifying accountable owners, source/contract evidence and independent closure tests. Include a claim the existing lab cannot establish even when its checks pass.

Solutions and evaluation criteria

Open complete solutions

  1. Origination adds 12 to gross loans and deposits, with no cash movement. The external transfer subtracts 5 from cash and aggregate deposits. The internal 7 transfer only changes which Alder customer owns the deposit. Net changes are cash −5, gross loans +12, deposits +7, total assets +7, liabilities +7 and equity 0. New cash is 29.5, gross loans 254, deposits 273, total assets 346.5, liabilities 333 and equity 13.5. Allowance remains 5 under the stipulated no-new-provision exercise. Actual underwriting might require an updated allowance; it is not inferred from this journal identity. Credit requires both counter-entries and the distinction between internal ownership transfer and external settlement.

  2. Provision is 5−6+8−1=6. One valid sequence is provision first (allowance 12, equity −6), then charge off 8 (gross 62, allowance 4), then recover 1 (cash +1, allowance 5). Final net loans are 62−5=57, versus initial 64: a fall of 7. Cash rises 1, so total assets and equity each fall 6. The charge-off draws on a sufficient allowance and leaves net loans unchanged at that step. A purported sequence charging off 8 from allowance 6 without first recognizing the shortfall is outside this positive-allowance model. Charging another 8 to income after the provision would misstate the final residual unless another valid, explained accounting entry existed. Credit requires the roll-forward, feasible sequence and asset/equity reconciliation.

  3. Eecon=34.5+56+L+6−326=L−229.5. Zero economic equity occurs at L=229.5. L=231 gives 1.5; L=223 gives −6.5. The complete L already values the portfolio's cash rights, including its credit assumptions; subtracting the book allowance again falsely gives −3.5 and −11.5. If L were instead a gross contractual amount or a valuation that explicitly omitted credit effects, it would need a separately justified adjustment, not automatically the accounting allowance. Credit requires stating the value basis and avoiding a legal insolvency claim from an unspecified mark.

  4. R=.70(237)+.20(60)+6=183.9. K remains 11.5 and U remains 337.5. Thus K/R≈6.2534%, which passes the toy 6% gate; K/U remains 3.4074%, which fails the 4% gate. Cash and both book/economic equity are unchanged. The new weighting classifies exposures differently; it has not supplied capital or changed promised borrower cash. A defensible real reclassification would require the applicable dated rule and supporting exposure/collateral/risk evidence, not a desire to improve the displayed ratio. The exercise does not establish that either weight estimates actual loss accurately.

  5. Cutoff 1 requires 30+10+36(1−h)≥70, so h≤1/6≈16.6667%. At h=.20 capacity is 28.8; base headroom is −1.2. Add the second receipt 12 and subtract deposits 5 to obtain 5.8; add 25 and subtract secured repayment 28.8(1.01)=29.088 to obtain 1.712. These later values assume the earlier gap somehow funded; they do not make the original plan feasible.

    Moving the 12 earlier changes the headrooms to 10.8,5.8,1.712. It removes the first failure without changing total receipts or the final balance. This is a changed contractual timing assumption, not permission to relabel a late receipt. For alternative haircut values, the later secured repayment must also use the changed drawn principal; one must not reduce the haircut while silently holding its debt repayment fixed.

  6. The risk ratio requires x≥.06(255)−11.5=3.8. Cash issuance enters its own exposure denominator: (11.5+x)/(337.5+x)≥.04 requires x≥25/12. Prefix liquidity requires x≥max(1.2,−5.8,−1.712,0)=1.2. The joint minimum is therefore 3.8, giving ratios 6% and 4.4829% and headrooms 2.6/9.6/5.512.

    Stable-deposit conversion of 3.8 gives equity 17.3, K 15.3, unchanged U 337.5 and ratios 6%/4.5333%, but unchanged cash headrooms and first failure. Borrowing 3.8 gives the cash headrooms of the cash issue, leaves K 11.5 and gives ratios 4.5098%/3.3695%; its later debt remains. The cash issue's severe economic equity is −6.5+3.8=−2.7. It solves the stated ratio and three-cutoff tests, not the severe valuation deficit, future funding after the horizon, actual regulatory approval or uncertain access to investors. Grade the separated mechanisms and scoped conclusion, not an unconditional recommendation to transact.

  7. Sale removes book 40 and brings cash 34, so its book loss is 6 and equity becomes 7.5. Compared with economic mark 36, selling for 34 destroys a further 2 of economic value, changing base economic equity 1.5 to −0.5. Do not subtract both the full book loss 6 and the mark-to-sale loss 2 from the original book or economic equity; they start from different bases.

    First headroom is 30+34+10−70=4. Next it is 4+12−5=11; finally 11+25=36, with no new secured debt repayment. The sale passes this cash plan while worsening both equity measures, and the supplied base economic residual becomes negative. The free pool has been sold and cannot also support the new 28.8 loan; counting both would require a different asset or explicitly different rights. The old pledged pool remains unavailable.

  8. The report improperly includes restricted cash 4.5, adds allowance 5 as though it were cash, and monetizes the already-pledged pool 20 at 80%, inventing another 16. The total overstatement is 4.5+5+16=25.5; correcting 24.3 gives actual first headroom −1.2. Book equity 13.5 does not establish usable cash or the economic value of loans and securities.

    A sound correction assigns finance to the allowance/gross/net loan and equity roll-forwards, treasury to settlement timestamps, cash restrictions and facility obligations, and credit/valuation staff to the loan marks and their evidence. An independent reviewer reproduces the ten-entry identity, validates that the same collateral is not counted twice, and tests each cash prefix including secured repayment. Source review must retain the 2013 document's historical UK scope and use an applicable dated accounting source for any current recognition claim. Passing code checks does not establish the actual recoverability of loans, lender performance, collateral rights or legal solvency. Evaluate the three quantified corrections, separation of valuation/cash questions, specific evidence and accountable independent closure; alternative role assignments earn credit if responsibilities are clear.

Teach-back and retention

Teach-back. Explain to a new treasurer why “we have five in the allowance” cannot fund a payment, and why converting a stable deposit into equity may help capital without helping today's settlement. A successful answer names both sides of each entry, the relevant deadline and whether the converted deposit was among the due outflows. Answer outline: an allowance reduces loan carrying value; spending it would invent cash. Conversion debits the deposit liability and credits equity with no reserve inflow. Only a separately changed obligation or actual cash receipt changes the specific settlement test.

Delayed check, without the tables. (1) With allowance 9 and a fully covered charge-off 4, what changes immediately? (2) A bank has unrestricted cash 6, receives 8 only tomorrow, and owes 7 today with no facility: what is today's gap? (3) If a fixed cash plan has headrooms (2,−3,1), what minimum up-front external cash makes every cutoff feasible? Answers: (1) gross loans and allowance each fall 4, net assets/equity/cash stay unchanged at that step; (2) 1, regardless of tomorrow's receipt; (3) 3, because it adds to every prefix. Revisit allowance entries or prefix feasibility if any distinction is lost.

Sources and the next step

The scoped sources are the 2013 Bank of England conceptual primer, the US 2020 interagency allowance statement and the BCBS 2008 liquidity principles. Source verification records the bodies and passages inspected; none supplies the chapter's fictional prices, haircut, policy thresholds or exercises. The lab reproduces a defined accounting and funding system, not a complete supervisory assessment.

Credit analysis and lending decisions next investigates the borrower cash that supports the bank's loan asset. Liquidity, funding and asset-liability management expands the simple cutoff test into richer maturity and contingent-funding scenarios. These extensions need new evidence and assumptions; a balanced ledger is the starting point for that work.

Sources and further study

  • Marc Farag, Damian Harland and Dan Nixon — Bank capital and liquidity (Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin, 2013 Q3, pp. 201–215) — Historical UK central-bank conceptual primer for bank balance-sheet funding, equity versus deployable cash, valuation bases and high-level ratio denominators. Original chapter ledger, definitions, calculations and exercises supply their own assumptions.
  • OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC and NCUA — Interagency Policy Statement on Allowances for Credit Losses (United States, 1 June 2020; 85 FR 32991) — Dated US accounting-policy context for a loss valuation account, provision changes, write-offs against the related allowance, forward-looking information and scope limits. The chapter uses a stipulated simple positive-allowance ledger, not a complete CECL implementation or current compliance certification.
  • Basel Committee on Banking Supervision — Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision (September 2008) — Historical international supervisory method context for timed cash obligations, operational/legal availability and avoiding reuse of encumbered collateral. Not a national-law definition, regulatory ratio calculation or claim that a central bank will lend. Additional c05 use: projected and contingent cash, collateral/transfer execution and contingency planning under explicitly fictional facility terms.
